proposed_correction.title: 2025 Law Adds Six-Month Medicaid Expansion Renewals and Shortens Retroactive Coverage

date_correction.basis: The law was signed on July 4, 2025; the cited eligibility and coverage provisions take effect later.

proposed_correction.description_short: P.L. 119-21 requires six-month renewals for Medicaid expansion adults and shortens, but does not end, retroactive coverage.
proposed_correction.description_medium: Signed July 4, 2025, P.L. 119-21 requires states to redetermine Medicaid eligibility for expansion adults every six months for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026. Effective January 1, 2027, it limits retroactive coverage to one month for expansion adults and two months for other Medicaid and CHIP applicants. The law narrows this coverage; it does not abolish it.
proposed_correction.description_long: President Donald Trump signed P.L. 119-21 on July 4, 2025. Among its Medicaid changes, the law requires states to redetermine eligibility every six months for adults enrolled through the Affordable Care Act expansion, applying to renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026. A separate provision, effective January 1, 2027, shortens the period of medical expenses that Medicaid may cover retroactively: to one month before application for expansion adults and two months for other Medicaid eligibility groups. The law also reduces the permitted retroactive coverage period for CHIP to two months. These provisions restrict, rather than end, retroactive coverage. KFF and the Congressional Research Service summarize the statutory requirements and effective dates. Their coverage estimates are projections and do not establish that a particular enrollee has already lost coverage or quantify realized enrollment effects. This entry describes what the law requires and when the provisions take effect; it does not present projected harms as observed outcomes.

supports: P.L. 119-21 requires six-month eligibility redeterminations for Medicaid expansion adults for renewals scheduled on or after December 31, 2026.
Section 71112 limits retroactive Medicaid coverage to one month for expansion adults and two months for traditional enrollees beginning January 1, 2027.
limits: Supports statutory requirements and KFF coverage estimates, not a specific realized coverage loss.

unresolved_gaps: The supplied sources do not establish implementation outcomes or a specific realized coverage loss; the description therefore states statutory requirements only.
notes: The former claim that retroactive coverage ends is inaccurate. The staged draft's reference to impacts from the prior unwinding is omitted because the cited sources do not establish those effects for this law.

proposed_correction.title: Rep. Andy Ogles Introduces Proposal to Allow a Third Presidential Election

date_correction.basis: Ogles's announcement and H.J.Res.29 introduction are dated January 23, 2025.

proposed_correction.description_short: Rep. Andy Ogles introduced a third-term constitutional amendment proposal on January 23, 2025.
proposed_correction.description_medium: On January 23, 2025, Rep. Andy Ogles introduced H.J.Res.29, proposing to amend the 22nd Amendment so a person could be elected president up to three times, subject to its consecutive-term limits. Ogles said the measure would let Donald Trump seek another term. He was the resolution's listed sponsor; the sources do not show an August 29 coalition introduction.
proposed_correction.description_long: Representative Andy Ogles of Tennessee introduced House Joint Resolution 29 on January 23, 2025. The proposal would amend the 22nd Amendment to permit a person to be elected president up to three times, while retaining a limit on being elected to an additional term after two consecutive terms. Ogles's announcement explicitly presented the proposal as a way for Donald Trump to serve another term. Congress.gov lists Ogles as the sponsor and records referral to the House Judiciary Committee on the same date. The record supports a single-member introduction, not a coalition of Republican lawmakers introducing the measure on August 29. The resolution's introduction establishes that a constitutional amendment was proposed; it does not establish that Congress adopted it or that it had sufficient support to pass. This corrected entry identifies the sponsor, proposal, and introduction date without adding unsupported claims about a later coalition or its chances in Congress.

proposed_correction.title: Iran Fires Missiles at Israel After Israel Begins June 2025 Attack

date_correction.basis: Reuters dated the initial Iranian missile barrage June 13, 2025.

proposed_correction.description_short: Iran fired its first missiles toward Israel on June 13, 2025, after Israel began strikes on Iran.
proposed_correction.description_medium: Iran launched missiles toward Israel on June 13, 2025, after Israel began its attack campaign against Iranian targets. Reuters reported that fewer than 100 missiles were fired in the initial barrage and that most were intercepted, according to the Israeli military. The U.S. strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities occurred later in June, so they did not trigger this first Iranian attack.
proposed_correction.description_long: On June 13, 2025, Iran launched missiles toward Israel after Israel began a campaign of strikes against Iranian nuclear and military targets. Reuters reported that fewer than 100 missiles were fired in the initial Iranian barrage and that most were intercepted or fell short, citing the Israeli military. This sequence matters: the first Iranian missile attack followed Israel's opening strikes. U.S. forces attacked Iranian nuclear facilities later in June, after the initial exchange had begun. Those later U.S. strikes therefore cannot be described as the trigger for the June 13 barrage. The cited report documents the reported count and immediate sequence, but the figure is attributed to the Israeli military rather than presented as an independently verified total. This entry is limited to the first reported Iranian missile attack and its timing; it does not summarize the subsequent exchanges or imply that the first barrage ended the conflict.

proposed_correction.title: Trump Commutes Kwame Kilpatrick's Federal Sentence, Leaving His Convictions Intact

date_correction.basis: The executive grant is dated January 13; the White House announced it on January 20.

proposed_correction.description_short: Trump commuted former Detroit mayor Kwame Kilpatrick's sentence in January 2021; the action did not erase his convictions.
proposed_correction.description_medium: Trump signed a commutation of former Detroit mayor Kwame Kilpatrick's remaining federal sentence on January 13, 2021; the White House announced it on January 20. The action reduced his prison sentence and was followed by his release, but it did not pardon him or erase his convictions. The reviewed sources do not establish whether the decision bypassed DOJ's traditional clemency review.
proposed_correction.description_long: President Donald Trump signed an executive grant commuting the remaining federal prison sentence of former Detroit mayor Kwame Kilpatrick on January 13, 2021. The White House announced the action on January 20 and described Kilpatrick's convictions for a racketeering and bribery scheme while he was mayor. The Justice Department's clemency record and the signed grant identify the action as a commutation, and the Associated Press reported that Kilpatrick was released after it. A commutation reduces or ends a sentence; it does not vacate the underlying convictions or make the recipient legally pardoned. The original title incorrectly called the action a pardon and used the announcement date as if it were the date of the grant. The sources document the executive action and public explanation but do not establish whether the administration bypassed the Justice Department's ordinary clemency review process. This entry therefore corrects the legal term and dates without making an unsupported claim about how the recommendation was processed.

proposed_correction.title: Wallets Linked to $TRUMP Token Creators Accumulated Nearly $100 Million in Trading Fees

date_correction.basis: Reuters estimated the fee accumulation over the token's first two weeks, January 17–30, 2025.

proposed_correction.description_short: Reuters estimated creator-linked $TRUMP wallets accumulated $86–100 million in fees; it could not trace personal proceeds to Trump.
proposed_correction.description_medium: Reuters estimated that three wallets linked to the $TRUMP token's creators accumulated roughly $86 million to $100 million in trading fees from January 17 through January 30, 2025. The report did not establish who ultimately received those fees or how much, if any, reached Donald Trump personally. Trading fees are not the same as realized personal profit.
proposed_correction.description_long: Reuters analyzed blockchain activity associated with the $TRUMP memecoin and estimated that three wallets linked to the token's creators accumulated about $86 million to $100 million in trading fees during its first two weeks, from January 17 through January 30, 2025. The estimate concerns fees associated with creator-linked wallets, not a confirmed personal payment to Donald Trump. Reuters said it could not determine the ultimate recipients or what share, if any, reached Trump because the relevant ownership and distribution arrangements were opaque. Fees generated by trading also differ from an individual's realized profit: a wallet balance or fee estimate does not by itself show who controlled the funds, whether they were withdrawn, or how they were distributed. The original record's title treated an estimate of project-related fees as more than $100 million in personal profit while president. This corrected entry retains the reported scale and time period but attributes the estimate to Reuters and identifies its limits. It does not infer personal proceeds from wallet association alone.

proposed_correction.title: Trump Signs Childhood-Vaccine Order and Discusses Autism in August 2026 Remarks

date_correction.basis: Executive Order 14420 and the signing transcript are dated August 10, 2026.

proposed_correction.description_short: Trump signed a childhood-vaccine order on August 10, 2026, and made autism-related remarks; WHO's review found no causal link.
proposed_correction.description_medium: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 revising federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including separate MMR components when available and spacing visits. At the signing, he discussed autism. A WHO review of evidence through 2025 found that rigorous studies do not support a causal association between vaccines and autism. The order and the scientific evidence are distinct.
proposed_correction.description_long: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420, which directs changes to federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including separate administration of measles, mumps, and rubella components when available and spacing some immunizations across visits. At the signing, Trump discussed autism and childhood vaccination. The executive order documents a policy action and the presidential transcript records his remarks; neither is scientific evidence that vaccines cause autism. The World Health Organization's review of evidence through 2025 found that the most methodologically rigorous studies do not support a causal association between vaccines, including thiomersal-containing vaccines, and autism spectrum disorder. The order was signed by Trump, not by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. This correction therefore changes the event date from 2025 to August 10, 2026, distinguishes the order's recommendations from the president's rhetoric, and separates both from the scientific evidence. It does not treat the signing itself as proof of a vaccine-autism link.
